questions.q: What is the primary architectural difference between a U-Net and a Diffusion Transformer (DiT) regarding how they process information?
options: U-Net uses global attention while DiT uses local convolutional filters.
U-Net processes images in a hierarchical, local manner, whereas DiT uses global attention where every token can interact with every other token.
DiT processes images in a hierarchical manner, while U-Net treats the entire canvas as a single token.
U-Net is permutation-invariant by default, while DiT requires no positional embeddings.
questions.answer: U-Net processes images in a hierarchical, local manner, whereas DiT uses global attention where every token can interact with every other token.
questions.why: The lesson states: 'In CU-301, we looked at the U-Net... that processes images in a hierarchical, local manner... But in CU-303... We are replacing the U-Net with a Transformer. Why? Because attention is not local; it is global. Every token can talk to every other token.'

questions.q: In the context of DiT blocks, what is the specific function of the AdaLN (Adaptive Layer Normalization) mechanism?
options: It replaces the attention mechanism with a convolutional layer to reduce computational cost.
It transforms the diffusion timestep into scale and shift parameters that modulate the features inside the transformer blocks.
It calculates the positional embeddings for the tokens to ensure spatial awareness.
It splits the input tensor into separate query, key, and value projections for the text stream.
questions.answer: It transforms the diffusion timestep into scale and shift parameters that modulate the features inside the transformer blocks.
questions.why: The lesson explains: 'The AdaLN mechanism takes this time information and transforms it into scale and shift parameters. These parameters are then applied to the features inside every transformer block.'

questions.q: Given a 512px image, a VAE downsample factor of 8, and a patch size of 2, how many tokens are generated for the DiT sequence?
questions.why: The lab results section states: 'For a 512px image, the VAE produces a 64 x 64 latent. With 2 x 2 patches, this becomes 32 x 32 = 1024 tokens.'

questions.q: Why is the 'identity' property of the AdaLN modulation function (where scale and shift are zero) considered crucial for stability?
options: It ensures that the model always generates high-frequency details regardless of the noise level.
It guarantees that if the timestep embedding were zero, the block acts as a pass-through, preserving the input features.
It allows the model to ignore the text embedding entirely during the denoising process.
It reduces the computational complexity of the attention mechanism from N^2 to N.
questions.answer: It guarantees that if the timestep embedding were zero, the block acts as a pass-through, preserving the input features.
questions.why: The lesson states: 'The "identity" case occurs when scale is 0 and shift is 0... This property is crucial for stability; if the timestep embedding were zero, the block would act as a pass-through, preserving the input features.'

questions.q: In the MM-DiT (Multimodal DiT) architecture, how does the attention mechanism differ from a standard DiT?
options: MM-DiT uses only self-attention for both image and text, ignoring cross-attention.
MM-DiT maintains separate query, key, and value projections for image and text streams, allowing bidirectional flow between them.
MM-DiT replaces the transformer blocks with convolutional layers to handle multimodal data.
MM-DiT does not use AdaLN modulation, relying instead on fixed layer normalization.
questions.answer: MM-DiT maintains separate query, key, and value projections for image and text streams, allowing bidirectional flow between them.
questions.why: The lesson states: 'In MM-DiT... the architecture extends this by maintaining separate query, key, and value projections for image and text streams... MMDiTJointAttention to handle the bidirectional flow between text and image tokens.'
